content: Borates in chemistry are chemical compounds that contain boron atoms bonded to three oxygen atoms, represented as B(OR)3. In the B(OR)4− anion, the number of oxygen atoms increases to four. The borate ion itself is BO3^3−, and it forms salts when combined with metallic elements. In nature, boron is commonly found as borate minerals. Additionally, boron can combine with silicate to form complex borosilicate minerals, such as tourmalines. Borate exists in various forms. Under acidic and near-neutral conditions, it primarily exists as boric acid, which is commonly written as H3BO3 but is more accurately represented as B(OH)3. At 25°C, its solubility is approximately 0.025 mol/L. One of the most well-known borate ions is the tetraborate ion, which is found in the mineral borax. Although boric acid reacts with hydroxide ions to form B(OH)4−, for pKa values and other calculations, it is often more convenient to use hypothetical ions. In the case of a typical polyprotic acid, the deprotonation series can be represented as dihydrogen borate, hydrogen borate, and borate as the pH increases. Boric acid can also form a variety of polymeric ions. The tetraborate ion, B4O7^2−, is particularly common, but other ions such as the hydrogen tetraborate ion (HB4O7−), triborate, and pentaborate are also observed. Metaborate ions, which have the empirical formula BO2−, form metaborate compounds. The formation of these complex, potentially infinite network structures is extensive and is perhaps only surpassed by silicates. Common borate salts include sodium metaborate (NaBO2) and sodium tetraborate (Na2B4O7). Sodium tetraborate also occurs naturally as the hydrated mineral borax (Na2B4O7·10H2O). Significant borax deposits are found in Boron, California, which is a major site for borate mining. The Atacama Desert in Chile also contains mineable concentrations of borates. Various forms of borates are used as wood preservatives or fungicides, such as disodium octaborate tetrahydrate. Borate esters are organic compounds of the type B(OR)3, where R represents an organic residue, such as an alkyl or aryl group. Examples of borate esters include trimethyl borate (B(OCH3)3), which is used as a precursor for boronic esters in Suzuki coupling reactions.
